newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Cash piles up at Swiss funds despite Holocaust row.
newsitem.headline: Cash piles up at Swiss funds despite Holocaust row.

text.p: The mountain of cash at Swiss bank investment funds continues to grow despite the crisis over the lost money of Jews murdered by Hitler, new statistics showed on Monday.

Fund statistician Bopp ISB said combined assets of public mutual funds set up by Swiss banks at home and abroad and sold mainly to international clients grew by 17 billion Swiss francs ($11 billion) to 261.7 billion at the end of June over a year ago.
The data points to continuing growth in new money flowing into Swiss mutual funds with net inflows of 1.57 billion Swiss francs in June after May's 1.5 billion and March's 1.8 billion.
The annual figure compares to total mutual fund assets of 251.4 billion Swiss francs at the end of May, which was up 16.4 billion over a year ago according to Bopp ISB data.

These are just about the only figures released on mutual fund assets in Switzerland's notoriously secretive banking industry, which has an estimated $1.8 trillion in private assets under management according to bank surveys.

Bankers said there was no sign the conflict over wartime accounts was hurting new money going to mutual funds and reported strong inflows from Latin America and Far East as well as from Germany, reflecting similar trends on private wealth flows into Swiss banks.
"The Holocaust crisis is not hurting business. Politics is one thing, money is something else. Business is business," said one Swiss banker who declined to be named.
Nicholas Fliess of Intrag, the company managing mutual funds for Union Bank of Switzerland, said assets of the bank's fund family grew by a net 3.5 billion Swiss francs since end-1996.

UBS, with the second biggest market share with 26 percent after Swiss Bank Corporation's 30 percent, set up three new open-ended global equity funds in June to meet high demand and the funds have attracted more than 800 million Swiss francs in total in assets so far, Fliess told Reuters.
Money market funds saw net outflows in June while bond, equities and asset allocation funds had net inflows, he added.
